new_statements.translation: 1.4.2.1 Basic rule: As a basic rule one can state that the vCC or v̄C nearest to the end of the word receives the accent: 'amátt 'Really! Certainly!' (speech of the Jews), saráḥt 'I went' (S), sárḥuk id. (N [= an-Naḏīr, Jabal Rāziḥ]), sáfaruk 'I travelled' (N), sāfárt id. (MJ). Also in forms like yiharrijū, yiktasū, madrasah I mostly [heard] the accent [on the first syllable]; stress of the Cairene type (also found in Yemeni dialects), yiharríjū, yiktásū, was rarer. 1.4.2.2 Final long vowels - e.g. in verbal and pronominal forms - never carry the accent: sáfarū 'they travelled', 'áni 'I'. ... 1.4.2.4 CvCvC: here Cv́CvC is always stressed ... 1.4.2.5 CvCvCvC: here too the first syllable is mostly stressed: kásilah 'lazy (f.)', bágarah 'cow', gútilan 'she was killed'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Arabic-type quantity-sensitive stress: the rightmost heavy sequence (short vowel + two consonants, or long vowel + consonant) in the word is stressed; word-final long vowels do not count and are never stressed; if the word has no such heavy sequence (CvCvC, CvCvCvC(v), yiktasu-type), stress falls on the first syllable (Cairene-type penult stress madrásah/yiktásū heard only rarely). Razih (siglum N, an-Naḏīr) forms cited under the rule: sárḥuk 'I went', sáfaruk 'I travelled'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the passages seen.
new_statements.exceptions: §1.4.2.3 (p.17) nominal forms with two long vowels stress the FIRST v̄C (ṣā́būn, ṣā́lūn, bā́būr, masā́mīr, mafā́tīḥin), only talātī́n 'thirty' mostly final; in Sāgēn bittihá heard beside bíttihā; §1.4.2.5 in (W) fluctuation wuṣílit ~ bágarah; §1.4.2.6 (p.18) in (M) im-Maṭṭah the accent moves one syllable rightward when object suffixes are added (gáhwan -> gahwánūh, réytum -> reytúmūh), and in (Ṣ) Ṣaʿdah and (W) the feminine ending -it is stressed before object suffixes as in Cairene (ḍarabíteh; also p.29 for the 3fsg -it); p.16: less accent fluctuation than Diem 1973 reported, and accent rules often have to be stated per morphological category rather than as general phonological rules.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for the Arabic dialects of the whole Ṣaʿdah region (Part A, general phonology), with elicited/cited word forms tagged by locality sigla; two of the five Grundregel examples are from (N) = an-Naḏīr on Jabal Rāziḥ (the Rāziḥīt-speaking market town; atlas point 29 'an-Nadir' = 'J. Rāziḥ'). The book's dedicated an-Naḏīr sketch (Part B, from p.131; phonology pp.~131-141) lists no separate Akzent subsection in its table of contents (p. xv), implying the regional rule holds; its Rāziḥ texts (pp.169-170) carry accent marks (wa-tráguk, ṭáttala, rukbuk). Read from snippet windows, not continuous pages.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted rule is Behnstedt's regional 'Grundregel' for the Arabic dialects of the Ṣaʿdah area (Part A of the book), not a Rāziḥ-only statement; it is illustrated inter alia with forms tagged (N) = an-Naḏīr, the market town on Jabal Rāziḥ whose speech Watson et al. (2006) call Rāziḥīt (Glottolog jaba1234; Behnstedt 1987 map point 29 'an-Nadir'/'J. Rāziḥ', Behnstedt 2016 atlas point 229 'Rāziḥ'). Behnstedt treats an-Naḏīr as a (k-perfect) Arabic dialect of the region and gives it its own sketch (pp.131ff) without a separate accent section; Glottolog instead classifies Jabal Razih as Modern Sayhadic. Other sigla in the passage: (Ṣ) Ṣaʿdah town, (MJ) Majz, (M) im-Maṭṭah, (S) Sāgēn, (W) -- i.e. the same rule also documents Ṣaʿdah-area North Yemeni Arabic.
